steps.html:
By the age of sixty the average person will have spent more than a year of waking life standing in queues. Two texts about the hours nobody can account for, and the two forms English uses to look further ahead than tomorrow.

  • Use the future continuous and the future perfect
  • Use collocations with time and money

steps.title: Text A · The fund nobody manages
steps.html:
Written for this course, using life-expectancy and time-use arithmetic from the American Time Use Survey.

Ask somebody where their money will be in thirty years and they will usually have an answer. There will be a pension, possibly an inheritance, some vague expectation about healthcare costs, and a figure they have looked up more than once. Ask the same person how they will be spending their Tuesday evenings in 2055 and the question sounds absurd. We think ahead about money as a matter of course. We take time for granted, and by the time we notice, we will already have spent most of it.

The arithmetic is not complicated. If you are thirty now, you will have lived roughly eleven thousand days and, on current life expectancy in most of Europe, you will live perhaps another nineteen thousand. Subtract sleep and work and the commute, and the discretionary hours — the ones nobody else has a claim on — come to something in the region of four a day. By the time you are seventy you will have accumulated more than fifty thousand of them. By then you will also have been working for something like forty-five years, and you will still not have decided what the evenings are for. That is a larger fund than most people’s savings, and almost nobody manages it.

People who throw their money around are considered foolish; people who throw their hours around are considered normal, and the only real difference is that nobody sends you a statement. A bank will tell you what you spent last month and what it left you with. Nothing performs that service for a Sunday afternoon. Next Sunday will be disappearing in exactly the same way, and by Monday you will have forgotten what happened to it. This is why the hours disappear without an argument: not because anyone decides to waste them, but because nothing in the system makes the loss visible while there is still time to do something about it.

steps.title: Text B · The two-to-five-hour finding
steps.html:
Written for this course, from Sharif, Mogilner & Hershfield, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 121(4), 2021.

The obvious conclusion is that more free time must be better, and the research says otherwise. In 2021 three researchers at Wharton and UCLA examined responses from more than 35,000 Americans, most drawn from the American Time Use Survey, plus two experiments of their own. Well-being rose as daily discretionary time increased, levelled off after about two hours, and then began to fall again beyond roughly five. Too little time produces stress. Too much, the authors argue, produces something else: a lacking sense of productivity and purpose. Most readers will be living somewhere inside that curve.

Almost everyone will have met that finding by the time they stop working. Anyone who retires at sixty-five will be handling eight or nine unstructured hours a day, every day, for perhaps twenty years. By the end of the first decade they will have spent more waking hours in retirement than in the whole of secondary school and university combined. The people who cope best, according to the same research, are not those with the most flexibility but those whose extra hours go into something worthwhile — and time with others counts. By seventy-five they will have made that decision some three thousand times.

The practical advice that follows is duller than it sounds. Do not while away the hours waiting for a better use to appear; it will not. Do not kill time and call it resting, because the two feel quite different afterwards. Take your time over things that repay it, and put a limit on the things that do not. Above all, stay in contact: the friendships people lose are almost never ended deliberately, and once you have lost touch with somebody for five years you will usually have lost them for good, while still meaning to call. In twenty years you will not be remembering the evenings you filled efficiently, but whether you made the most of the ones that mattered.

steps.title: future continuous and future perfect
steps.html:
Two forms for looking further ahead than tomorrow.

Future continuous — will be + -ing — describes something in progress at a point in the future. This time next year you will be doing more or less what you are doing now. It answers: what will be going on then?

It also has a second, very common use: a neutral prediction about an arrangement, with no intention implied. I'll be seeing her on Thursday anyway means 'that is simply how things fall', not 'I have decided to see her'.

Future perfect — will have + past participle — stands at a point in the future and looks back at what is already complete by then. By the time you finish this page, you will have spent four minutes on it.

There is a continuous version too — will have been + -ing — for how long something will have gone on: By June I will have been working here for ten years.

Both forms almost always need a time marker: by, by the time, this time next year, in ten years' time, by the age of sixty. Without one, neither form makes sense.

steps.title: Example bank.
steps.html:
Twelve sentences from the two texts.

By the time you finish this page, you will have spent four minutes on it.
Complete by a future point.

By tonight you will have lost roughly two hours.
By + a future time.

At the end of ten years you will have answered a great many messages.
Looking back from ten years ahead.

This time next year you will be doing what you are doing now.
In progress at that point.

By the age of sixty the average person will have spent a year in queues.
A striking use of the future perfect with a statistic.

Decide what you will be doing at seven on Tuesday.
In progress at a named moment.

By June I will have been working here for ten years.
Duration up to a future point.

I'll be seeing her on Thursday anyway.
Neutral — no intention implied.

By the time you finish, the shop will have closed.
Present after by the time.

In ten years' time nobody will be using these machines.
In ten years' time is the marker.

She won't have finished by Friday.
Negative future perfect.

Will you be using the car this evening?
A very common, non-pushy way of asking.

steps.title: Choosing between the two future forms
steps.html:
1. The facts: you started this job in June 2016. It is now 2026. Somebody asks about next June.
  2. If the question is how long, use the future perfect continuous: By next June I will have been working here for ten years.
  3. If the question is what will be finished, use the future perfect: By next June I will have completed ten years.
  4. If the question is what will be going on at that moment, use the future continuous: This time next June I will be working on the same floor.
  5. Check the time marker is there. Remove by next June and none of the three sentences works. And note the trap: after by the time, use the present — by the time you read this, never will read.

steps.title: Write your piece.
steps.sub: 140–170 words. Use the future continuous at least twice and the future perfect at least twice, each with a time marker.
steps.html:
• Open with a time marker and something that will be complete.
  • Use the future perfect continuous once, for how long.
  • Say what will be going on at that point, with the future continuous.
  • Say one thing you will <i>not</i> have done.
  • Close with what you would rather happened.

Useful language

  • This time next year I will be …
  • By the end of … I will have …
  • By then I will have been …-ing for …
  • I will probably still be …
  • What I will not have done is …
  • By the time I …, I hope to have …
steps.modelHtml:
This time in five years

By the summer of 2031 I will have been teaching for twelve years, which is longer than I expected to stay in anything. By then I will also have finished the second qualification, assuming the funding survives.

What I will be doing at that point is harder to guess. I will probably still be living in the same city — my mother is here and I am not going to move while that is true. I imagine I will be working fewer hours and complaining about it more.

What I will not have done is start the school I keep describing to people at dinner. By the time I am forty I will either have made a serious attempt at it or stopped mentioning it. I would rather it was the first.
